peer.body: Because Python optimisation mode (`-O`) removes `assert` statements, an unexpected message type under `-O` would silently fall off the end of `listen_for_disconnect` returning `None`, which then propagates as `done.result() is None` and is sent to `send_response` — producing a much more confusing failure than the intended loud error. Felixxm already suggested raising `ValueError` here; given assertions can be compiled out, that suggestion is worth honoring even though this is a 'should never happen' case.
peer.rationale: The whole point of this branch is to be loud on a protocol violation. `assert` undermines that under `-O`. A plain `raise ValueError(...)` is the same number of lines and preserves the invariant unconditionally.

unmatched_peer.body:
`asyncio.wait(..., return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)` only guarantees that *at least* one task is done — it does not guarantee that *exactly* one is. If `run_get_response` and `listen_for_disconnect` happen to complete in the same event-loop iteration (e.g., the view finishes just as a disconnect arrives), both end up in `done` and `pending` is empty. The subsequent `pending.pop()` then raises `KeyError` and the response is never sent, leaking the response from `run_get_response` and surfacing an opaque error to the protocol server.

Consider iterating `pending` (it may be empty) and handling the case explicitly, e.g. cancel/await every task in `pending` and pick the response-bearing one from `done`.
unmatched_peer.rationale: FIRST_COMPLETED semantics permit multiple completions per wait, and the current unpacking will KeyError in that edge case. Even if rare in practice, an ASGI handler that occasionally crashes with KeyError under tight races is hard to debug.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: `done.pop()/pending.pop()` can raise KeyError when both tasks finish in the same loop iteration

unmatched_peer.body: `body_file.close()` is invoked on every error branch (invalid request, RequestAborted, AssertionError) but not on the happy path. This mirrors the previous code, but with the refactor it's worth re-confirming intent — the `SpooledTemporaryFile` will be cleaned up when the request object is GC'd, but explicit cleanup (e.g. via `try/finally` or relying on response close) is preferable for long-lived processes. Worth at least a comment documenting that the request/response lifecycle takes ownership.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Refactors are a good moment to make implicit cleanup explicit; future maintainers reading the four explicit `body_file.close()` calls will reasonably wonder why the success path differs.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: `body_file` not closed on the success path

unmatched_peer.body: `hello_with_delay` adds a full second to `test_delayed_disconnect_with_body`. A shorter sleep (e.g. 0.5s or less, matching the disconnect-await timeout in the handler test) would still exercise the 'view still running when disconnect arrives' scenario without bloating CI time. Django's test suite already has many `asyncio`-related slow tests; new ones should err on the side of speed.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Test suite wall-clock time matters; a 1s sync sleep in a sync view that's only used to demonstrate 'view is still running' can be considerably shorter.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Hard-coded `time.sleep(1)` makes the suite slower

unmatched_peer.body: `await asyncio.sleep(0.1)` to 'let the view actually start' before sending the disconnect is fragile — on a heavily loaded CI runner the view may not have reached its own `await asyncio.sleep(0.2)` within 100ms, and on a fast machine the view may finish before the disconnect is processed if the sleeps were ever tuned. Consider synchronising via an `asyncio.Event` set inside the view, so the test waits deterministically for the view to be in-flight before disconnecting.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Time-based synchronisation in async tests is a known source of flakes in Django's suite. Event-based handshakes are cheap and deterministic.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Timing-sensitive `await asyncio.sleep(0.1)` will be flaky on busy CI

unmatched_peer.body: The example tells users to catch `asyncio.CancelledError`, but does not explain that this exception can be raised for reasons other than client disconnect (task cancellation from the event loop, server shutdown, nested `wait_for` timeouts, etc.). Encouraging users to `except asyncio.CancelledError` without that caveat may lead them to attribute every cancellation to a client disconnect. A one-line note that `CancelledError` indicates the request was cancelled (most commonly by client disconnect) and that the `raise` is required for proper cleanup would help.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The doc is the primary user-facing artifact for this feature. Misleading users into thinking CancelledError == disconnect can cause subtle bugs in cleanup code (e.g., updating UI/state assuming the client is gone when it isn't).
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Example doesn't make clear *why* `CancelledError` (rather than `RequestAborted`) is what views see

unmatched_peer.body: `test_assert_in_listen_for_disconnect` relies on `assert False, ...` actually firing. If Django is ever exercised under `python -O` (e.g. some downstream packagers), this test silently changes behaviour — the assertion is removed and `listen_for_disconnect` returns `None`, the handler tries to send `None` as a response, and the test fails with a much less helpful error. Switching the production code from `assert` to a real exception (see related comment) would also fix this test's fragility.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Pairs with the `-O` concern in the production code; calling it out near the test makes the connection explicit for reviewers.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Test will be flaky if `assert` is stripped under `-O`

unmatched_peer.body:
The final `body_file.close()` is unconditional, but it is only reached if every iteration of the `for task in tasks:` loop completes without raising. The only exceptions explicitly handled are `RequestAborted`, `AssertionError`, and `asyncio.CancelledError`. If `process_request` raises anything else (e.g. an error from `send_response`, or an unhandled exception that escapes `get_response_async`/middleware), `task.result()` will re-raise inside the loop, the second task will never be cancelled/awaited, and `body_file` will never be closed — producing the same `ResourceWarning` on 3.12+ that @felixxm patched around elsewhere in this PR, plus a stranded pending task.

Wrapping the wait+cleanup in `try/finally` (or restoring the `with body_file:` context manager that was discussed earlier in review) would make the resource handling robust against any failure path, instead of relying on enumerating which exception types can occur.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The previous implementation only had to worry about exceptions from a single `run_get_response` task and still explicitly closed `body_file` in both error branches. The new code merges send_response into the same task, broadening the set of possible exceptions, but narrowed the cleanup to a single unconditional `close()` at the bottom that any raise will skip. This is a latent resource leak.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: body_file can leak if an unexpected exception escapes the task-cleanup loop

unmatched_peer.body: With the unconditional `body_file.close()` at line 224, the explicit `body_file.close()` before `raise` in the `AssertionError` branch is dead code — except that, as noted in the sibling comment, the bottom `close()` is itself skipped when this `raise` fires, which is why it has to be duplicated here. Once the cleanup is moved into a `try/finally`, this branch collapses to a bare `raise` (or can be dropped entirely, letting the exception propagate naturally).
unmatched_peer.rationale: Reducing the number of places `body_file.close()` is invoked makes the resource lifecycle easier to audit and removes the asymmetry where AssertionError gets a `close()` but no other unexpected exception does.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: `body_file.close()` duplicated in AssertionError branch

unmatched_peer.body:
@felixxm noted earlier that `test_disconnect_both_return` and `test_streaming` pass without the production change, and @qxcv acknowledged that inducing simultaneous completion of both tasks is non-deterministic and only happens here as a side effect of `ApplicationCommunicator`'s internals. As written, this test will continue to pass even if the regression returns (i.e. if someone reverts to `pending.pop()`/`done.pop()`), so it does not protect the behavior the PR claims to fix.

Given the author's own assessment ("I'm inclined to rip out the extra test... and call it a day") and that the two-task-done branch is already exercised structurally by the loop, I'd recommend either dropping this test or adding a comment explaining that it's a smoke test only and the actual regression coverage lives in `test_streaming_disconnect` / `test_asyncio_streaming_cancel_error`.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Tests that pass equally with and without the patch under test are misleading: they imply coverage of the regression while providing none, and they will silently rot when the implementation changes.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: test_disconnect_both_return does not actually exercise the fix

unmatched_peer.body: `test_streaming` only verifies that a streaming view returns its two chunks — it does not interact with the disconnect machinery this PR is changing, and the happy path of `StreamingHttpResponse` over ASGI is already covered indirectly (e.g. `test_file_response`). The disconnect-specific behavior is what `test_streaming_disconnect` and `test_asyncio_streaming_cancel_error` cover. Per @felixxm's review, scope-creep tests should be split into a separate change so the diff for this fix stays focused.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Keeping the PR scope tight matters for backports (this is flagged as a 5.0 release blocker). Tests that are unrelated to the fix can either be dropped here and added in a follow-up, or be reframed (e.g. asserting that streaming chunks arrive between yields) to add real value.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: test_streaming overlaps with existing coverage and doesn't exercise the disconnect path

unmatched_peer.body: The text says "Django will cancel the coroutine that is handling the response." In the new handler, what is cancelled is the `process_request` task — which wraps both `run_get_response` (the view) and `send_response` (the body iteration). Saying "the coroutine handling the response" is correct for streaming iteration, but readers may not realize that the same cancellation reaches their async view body if it is still running. A small clarification, or a forward-reference to `async-handling-disconnect` here (in addition to the one at the bottom), would prevent users from thinking these are two different cancellation sources.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The mental model the docs paint matters because users will write `except asyncio.CancelledError` based on it. A more accurate description avoids surprises like "my view body got CancelledError, I thought only the streaming generator did".
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Docs slightly mischaracterize what is cancelled

unmatched_peer.body: The comment claims ordering matters because `listen_for_disconnect()` "should not raise unexpected errors that would prevent us from cancelling `process_request()`". But `process_request` is in the same list and the loop unconditionally iterates both tasks; an unexpected error from the first task would already break the second task's cleanup regardless of order (see the resource-leak comment). Either the ordering is load-bearing — in which case the loop should be restructured to guarantee both tasks get cancelled/awaited even on unexpected errors — or the comment is overstating its importance. Worth either tightening the cleanup logic so the order genuinely doesn't matter, or rewording the comment to describe the actual invariant.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Comments that describe a safety property the code doesn't actually enforce become misleading once they age. Either harden the code to match the comment, or weaken the comment to match the code.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Comment about ordering is structurally fragile

unmatched_peer.body: The type annotation `source_type: Type[BaseModel]` is incorrect for this example. In `Annotated[int, Metadata()]`, pydantic calls `Metadata.__get_pydantic_core_schema__` with `source_type=int`, which is not a `Type[BaseModel]`. Readers who copy this snippet and run a strict type checker (mypy/pyright) will get spurious errors, and it actively misleads them about what `source_type` can be in metadata classes. Use `Any` (or `type[Any]`) instead.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The whole point of the example is to teach a correct, copy-pastable pattern for attaching metadata to non-BaseModel fields. The current annotation contradicts the example's own usage (`state: Annotated[int, Metadata()]`), where `source_type` is `int`, not a BaseModel subclass.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Misleading `source_type` annotation in metadata example

unmatched_peer.body:
When `error_messages is None`, `self.error_messages` is assigned the same dict object as the class-level `default_error_messages`. Any later mutation (e.g. `paginator.error_messages['invalid_page'] = '...'`) silently mutates the class default for every other `Paginator` instance. Copy the defaults to be safe:

```python
self.error_messages = {
    **self.default_error_messages,
    **(error_messages or {}),
}
```

This also has the nice side effect of removing the conditional branch.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Shared mutable class attribute referenced by instances is a subtle aliasing bug. Django's own `Field` and `BaseValidator` patterns copy `default_error_messages` per-instance for exactly this reason.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Shared mutable default_error_messages dict

unmatched_peer.body: Django's convention elsewhere (`Field`, `BaseValidator`, `ModelForm`) is to walk the MRO and merge `default_error_messages` from each parent class, so subclasses can add a key without redeclaring all of them. Here, a `Paginator` subclass that sets `default_error_messages = {"my_key": ...}` will lose `invalid_page`/`min_page`/`no_results`. Worth considering the MRO-merge pattern for consistency, or at minimum documenting that subclasses must replicate the full dict.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Inconsistency with the established Django pattern for `default_error_messages` will surprise users subclassing Paginator and weakens the framework-level convention.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: default_error_messages does not follow MRO-merge pattern used elsewhere

unmatched_peer.body: The error messages are raised by `Paginator.validate_number()`; `Paginator.page()` only raises them transitively. Either reference `validate_number` or phrase as "raised by the paginator" for accuracy.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Minor doc accuracy: `page()` is the convenient public entry point but `validate_number()` is the actual raiser, and it is part of the public API and called directly in tests/users' code.
unmatched_peer.suggestion:
* The new :attr:`django.core.paginator.Paginator.error_messages` argument
  allows customizing the error messages raised by
  :meth:`.Paginator.validate_number`.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Release note wording: page() vs validate_number()

unmatched_peer.body: Worth noting which exception type each key produces so users can target their wording: `invalid_page` → `PageNotAnInteger`, `min_page` and `no_results` → `EmptyPage`. Also, the new strings the user supplies are not run through `gettext_lazy` automatically — a one-line note that users should wrap their overrides in `gettext_lazy` if they want i18n would prevent a common gotcha.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The keys are abstract; without mapping them to the exception classes (and noting the i18n wrapping) users will need to read the source to know what each one controls.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Document key→exception mapping and translation expectations

unmatched_peer.body: Consider also asserting that passing `error_messages=None` (the default) still produces the original messages, and that an unknown key in `error_messages` is accepted without error (current behavior — extra keys are silently merged in). Locking down both behaviors prevents accidental regressions if the merge strategy changes (see related comment about copying defaults).
unmatched_peer.rationale: The test covers the happy path and partial-override but not the no-arg or unknown-key edge cases that the merge implementation exposes.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Missing edge-case coverage for error_messages

unmatched_peer.body: Use `==` to compare `base.fullname` to `ROOT_MODEL_FULLNAME`, not `in`. The substring check is inconsistent with the very next analogous line (`is_settings = any(base.fullname == BASESETTINGS_FULLNAME for base in info.mro[:-1])`) and would false-match any class whose fullname happens to contain `pydantic.root_model.RootModel` as a substring (e.g., a re-exported alias or a user class named `RootModelFoo` placed in a similarly-named module). Switch to equality for consistency and safety.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Defensive consistency with the immediately following `is_settings` check, and to avoid spurious matches when a class fullname has the RootModel path as a substring.
unmatched_peer.suggestion: is_root_model = any(base.fullname == ROOT_MODEL_FULLNAME for base in info.mro[:-1])
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Use `==` instead of `in` when matching `ROOT_MODEL_FULLNAME`

unmatched_peer.body: `args[0].kind = ...` assumes that `args` is non-empty and that the first arg is `root`. For ordinary `RootModel` subclasses the inherited `root` field guarantees this, but if `collect_fields` returns an empty list for any edge case (e.g., a malformed subclass during incremental semantic analysis), this will raise `IndexError` from inside the mypy plugin and crash the checker rather than producing a friendly error. Guard the access (`if args:`) or assert that `args[0].variable.name == 'root'` before mutating. This also matches dmontagu's review note about needing to verify the default/shape of the arg before re-kinding it.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Defensive — a plugin crash inside mypy is worse than a missed optimization, and the index-zero assumption is implicit rather than enforced.
unmatched_peer.suggestion:
if is_root_model and args:
    # convert root argument to positional argument
    assert args[0].variable.name == 'root'
    args[0].kind = ARG_POS if args[0].kind == ARG_NAMED else ARG_OPT
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Guard `args[0]` access in `add_initializer` for `is_root_model`

unmatched_peer.body: The `api` parameter is typed as `CheckerPluginInterface`, but this helper is called from `PydanticModelTransformer.collect_fields`, where `self._api` is a `SemanticAnalyzerPluginInterface` (collection happens during semantic analysis, not type checking). Compare to the sibling `error_untyped_fields`, which is correctly typed as `SemanticAnalyzerPluginInterface`. The current annotation is misleading and would be wrong if any caller passes it the actual checker API. Change the annotation to `SemanticAnalyzerPluginInterface` (or the union used elsewhere) so it accurately reflects the call site.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Type annotation mismatch with the actual call context; will mislead future maintainers and would fail strict type-checking if exercised.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Wrong `api` type annotation on `error_extra_fields_on_root_model`

unmatched_peer.body: The test module covers the new error case (`pets: List[str]` on `Pets4`) but does not exercise a few important scenarios introduced by this PR: (1) explicitly overriding `root` in a subclass (e.g., `class PetsX(RootModel[List[str]]): root: List[int]`) should still be allowed and produce no error; (2) instantiation with `root=` keyword as well as positional should both be tested (the PR changes the kind to `ARG_POS`/`ARG_OPT`, which affects keyword-only usage); (3) `reveal_type(pets1.root)` to confirm the typed `root` attribute is still accessible. Adding these would lock in the intended behavior and prevent regressions when the args[0]-mutation logic is revisited.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The fixture as written only verifies the happy path and one negative case; the PR's two main behavioral changes (positional vs keyword root, error on extra fields) deserve broader coverage, especially given dmontagu's open questions on the diff.
unmatched_peer.issue_header: Broaden root_models.py mypy fixture coverage
